nasa: "Nasa" was a project to develop our teamwork and coding skills in line with agile programming. In this project we created a space-themed website that makes strong use of the possibilities offered by the API from Nasa but not only. We created four main functions: display of APOD images, a live map of disasters as seen from space, a comparison scale of asteroids that pass close to the earth and the possibility to see a star map of a selected constellation. In addition to this, we created the possibility of logging in and registering, so that users can create their own account and add photos of interest to the gallery, as well as a few smaller options such as charts with data from space, pages dedicated to individual planets and a map showing the position of other planets in relation to the Earth. For the website, we mainly used the Python language and its wide range of libraries, such as Sunpy, Folium and Astropy, and for the web page we used the Flask framework, as well as CSS and HTML. In this project, I was responsible, among other things, for managing the work, but also for implementing 3 of the 4 main features, a few minor ones and helping with the front-end.
chess: The "Chess" project was my final project in Java. I decided to build a solid foundation for a chess game, leveraging the object-oriented nature of the language. Each chess piece type was implemented as a separate class, inheriting from a common Piece superclass. Additionally, I designed key classes such as Chessboard, Move, and Game to efficiently manage the game state and validate legal moves.The project uses a dual-layer representation of the chessboard and pieces—while the board tracks piece positions at any given moment, each piece also maintains knowledge of its own location. This approach significantly simplifies move validation. The game fully supports advanced chess mechanics, including castling, en passant, and crucial game-ending conditions like check, checkmate, and stalemate.After completing the initial version, I decided to continue developing the project by adding a graphical user interface (GUI) and implementing a simple chess engine, allowing players to compete against a bot. Working on this project enhanced my object-oriented thinking, especially in larger applications where managing class interactions is essential. It also sparked my interest in chess programming, motivating me to keep improving the game.
prediction:
The "Computer Price Prediction" project was my final project in Python. Its goal was to develop a machine learning-based application that predicts the price of used computers based on specifications such as processor, RAM, storage type, graphics card, and overall condition.

The application integrates several key technologies, including web scraping, data preprocessing, a regression-based predictive model, and a graphical user interface (GUI). It automatically collects data from an online marketplace, processes it, and trains a model to estimate computer prices. Users can input system specifications, and the application provides a predicted price.

During development, I focused on a modular code structure to ensure clarity and scalability. The core components include data collection and processing, model training, and user interaction via a Tkinter-based GUI. The model was designed to be easily updated, allowing for improvements in prediction algorithms and data expansion from additional sources.

Working on this project deepened my understanding of machine learning applications in real-world scenarios and taught me efficient data processing and integration of multiple technologies into a single system. It also highlighted the importance of adapting ML models to real-world data and optimizing the prediction process, inspiring me to continue exploring this field.
dragon:
The "Dragon Brigade" project was my final project in C/C++. Its goal was to develop an RPG game where the player takes on the role of a member of the legendary Dragon Brigade, exploring the world, battling enemies, and making decisions that shape the story and determine the game's ending.

The gameplay integrates several key mechanics, including a quest system, turn-based combat, NPC interactions, inventory and economy mechanics, and a multi-threaded storyline with multiple endings. A crucial aspect of the game is using collected items and knowledge from books, allowing the player to discover new possibilities and influence character progression.

From a technical perspective, the project was developed in C/C++, with a focus on performance, object-oriented design, and code clarity. The game follows a modular structure, making it easy to expand and improve systems such as enemy AI, scripted events, and world interactions.

Working on this project taught me efficient memory management, game system design, and how to implement RPG mechanics in a low-level language. It was also a great experience in handling a large-scale project, requiring careful planning of component interactions and optimizing code for performance. This project motivated me to continue developing the game and exploring advanced game programming techniques.
fit:
The "FitTracker" project was my final project in mobile application development for Android. Its goal was to create an intuitive and functional workout management app, allowing users to schedule, edit, and track their physical activities. Additionally, the app provides notifications for scheduled workouts, helping users maintain consistency in their fitness routine.

From a technical perspective, FitTracker was developed in Kotlin, leveraging modern Android technologies such as Jetpack Compose (modern UI), Room (local database), LiveData & ViewModel (state management), and WorkManager (notification handling). The app enables users to schedule workouts, mark them as completed, review workout history, and delete stored activities.

Working on this project taught me efficient mobile app design, the application of MVVM architecture, local data management, and integrating Jetpack Compose with other Android components. FitTracker also helped me understand the importance of UI optimization and lifecycle management in mobile development. Future improvements may include cloud synchronization, Google Fit integration, and workout statistics analysis.
ml:
The "Machine Learning Projects" collection is a structured exploration of machine learning models, focusing on regression and classification techniques. The goal was to analyze different data preprocessing, feature engineering, and model evaluation methods while applying them to real-world datasets. The project consists of three Jupyter Notebooks, each addressing key aspects of machine learning:

ML_Regression.ipynb – Implementation and evaluation of regression models to predict numerical values.
ML_Classification.ipynb – Classification using various supervised learning algorithms and performance comparison.
Titanic.ipynb – Data exploration and classification model application to predict passenger survival on the Titanic dataset.
Additionally, I worked on a Kaggle project, Heart Attacks where I applied classification techniques to predict risk of heart attacks.

Throughout this project, I gained experience in data preprocessing, feature engineering, model selection, and evaluation. The implementation covered both traditional statistical models and advanced techniques, including ensembling and neural networks.

This project provided valuable insights into practical machine learning applications, model optimization, and the importance of data preparation. It serves as a solid foundation for further exploration of advanced predictive modeling techniques.
omni:
The "Omnioktagram" project was created at the request of my friend as a tool to support his original narrative campaign. The goal was to develop an interactive web application that allows users to draw spells based on an octogram — an eight-point magical structure. The user can draw lines between vertices, mark points, skip steps, and replay spells using numerical codes. Once the drawing is complete, a description of the spell’s effect and its mana cost are generated.

From a technical standpoint, Omnioktagram was built in JavaScript using HTML5 Canvas and a modular architecture (ES Modules). The project features dynamic coordinate recalculations, responsive interface scaling, support for both touch and mouse interactions, and a theme switcher (dark/light mode). The interface is minimalist and adapts to various screen sizes.

While working on this project, I learned how to design responsive web applications, manage application state without frameworks, create drawing systems based on relative coordinates, and design creative user interfaces. The Omnioktagram project taught me the importance of code clarity, UI consistency, and smooth performance in interactive applications. Future development may include saving spells to the cloud, multiplayer mode, or integration with narrative campaign systems.
mm:
The project "Multimodal Emotion Classifier" was developed as part of my bachelor’s thesis and focused on emotion recognition based on visual data (facial images) and acoustic data (speech spectrograms) derived from the IEMOCAP corpus. The main goal was to build a complete system capable of recognizing emotions using both modalities simultaneously, applying a multiplicative gating mechanism to dynamically weigh the contributions of audio and video signals.

The project included the full processing pipeline — from extracting data from raw audio-video recordings, through preprocessing and cleaning of input samples, to constructing and training a deep learning model in TensorFlow. Separate convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were designed for each modality and subsequently fused into a unified multimodal architecture. Input data were loaded as paired spectrogram–face samples, and the system was evaluated for its classification performance.

This work provided me with hands-on experience in handling multimodal datasets, integrating heterogeneous signals, designing fusion models, and applying modern techniques in image and signal processing for emotion classification tasks.
